q: An auditor sets planned audit risk at 5% for an assertion, assesses inherent risk at 80%, and assesses control risk at 50%. Using the audit risk model, what is the acceptable level of detection risk?
exp: Detection risk = AR / (IR x CR) = 0.05 / (0.80 x 0.50) = 0.05 / 0.40 = 12.5%. Dividing by inherent risk alone gives 6.25%, and multiplying all three factors gives 2%.

q: Tests of controls over purchasing reveal more deviations than expected, so the auditor raises the assessed control risk for the completeness of accounts payable. Which response is most appropriate?
choices: Increase acceptable detection risk and reduce the extent of substantive tests
Decrease acceptable detection risk, for example by performing more extensive substantive procedures at year-end rather than at an interim date
Leave detection risk unchanged, because control risk does not affect substantive procedures
Lower the assessed inherent risk to offset the higher control risk
exp: Detection risk moves inversely with the RMM. Higher control risk means acceptable detection risk must fall, so the auditor needs more persuasive substantive evidence through changes in nature, timing toward period-end, or extent. Inherent risk is assessed independently and cannot be lowered to offset control risk.

q: After performing risk assessment procedures, an auditor concludes that both inherent risk and control risk for the valuation of inventory are higher than in the prior year. Which component of audit risk can the auditor directly change in response?
choices: Inherent risk, by modifying the audit approach to inventory
Control risk, by recommending improvements to management
Detection risk, by changing the nature, timing, and extent of substantive procedures
The risk of material misstatement, by lowering performance materiality
exp: Inherent and control risk are characteristics of the entity that exist whether or not there is an audit. The auditor assesses them but does not control them. The auditor manages detection risk through the substantive procedures it designs and performs.

q: Under AU-C 315, as amended by SAS No. 145, an auditor does not plan to test the operating effectiveness of controls over an assertion. How should the auditor assess the risk of material misstatement for that assertion?
choices: Assess inherent risk separately and assess control risk at the maximum, so that the RMM equals the assessed inherent risk
Assess the RMM as a single combined risk, without separately assessing inherent risk
Assess control risk based on the design of controls evaluated during walkthroughs
Assess control risk at a low level if no deficiencies were identified in the prior year
exp: SAS No. 145 requires separate assessments of inherent risk and control risk at the assertion level. If the auditor does not plan to test operating effectiveness, control risk is assessed at the maximum, so the RMM is the inherent risk assessment. Design evaluation alone cannot support a lower control risk.

q: Which of the following risks must the auditor treat as a significant risk?
choices: An assessed risk of material misstatement due to fraud
The risk related to processing routine, high-volume cash receipts
Any risk in an account whose balance exceeds performance materiality
Any risk for which control risk is assessed at the maximum
exp: AU-C 240 requires the auditor to treat assessed risks of material misstatement due to fraud as significant risks. Routine, high-volume processing is usually lower in inherent risk, and neither account size nor maximum control risk alone makes a risk significant.

q: An auditor plans to respond to a significant risk related to the valuation of complex derivative instruments using only substantive procedures. Under AU-C 330, those procedures must include
choices: substantive analytical procedures, which are alone sufficient
inquiries of the treasury department and review of board minutes
tests of details
a review of the prior-year working papers for the same risk
exp: When the approach to a significant risk consists only of substantive procedures, AU-C 330 requires those procedures to include tests of details. Substantive analytical procedures alone are not sufficient for a significant risk.

q: An auditor uses 5% of pretax income from continuing operations as the benchmark for materiality and sets performance materiality at 75% of overall materiality. Pretax income from continuing operations is $2,400,000. What is performance materiality?
exp: Overall materiality = 5% x $2,400,000 = $120,000, and performance materiality = 75% x $120,000 = $90,000. The $120,000 figure is overall materiality, which is the common mistake of stopping one step early.

q: An auditor sets overall materiality at 1% of total assets of $40,000,000 and sets the clearly trivial threshold at 5% of overall materiality. Misstatements below what amount need not be accumulated?
exp: Overall materiality is 1% x $40,000,000 = $400,000, and clearly trivial is 5% x $400,000 = $20,000. Under AU-C 450, misstatements that are clearly trivial need not be accumulated. Using $400,000 confuses materiality with the much smaller clearly trivial threshold.

q: An auditor based preliminary materiality on forecast pretax income of $5,000,000. Late in the audit, actual pretax income is determined to be only $3,000,000. Under AU-C 320, the auditor should
choices: retain the preliminary materiality, because materiality is fixed once the audit plan is approved
increase materiality to reflect the greater uncertainty in the results
revise materiality and determine whether performance materiality and the nature, timing, and extent of further audit procedures remain appropriate
revise materiality only if management agrees to the revision
exp: AU-C 320 requires the auditor to revise materiality when information becomes known that would have led to a different amount initially. A lower materiality may require more audit work. Materiality is not fixed at planning, and management's agreement is irrelevant.

q: Under AU-C 320, when is it appropriate to set a materiality level lower than overall materiality for particular classes of transactions, account balances, or disclosures?
choices: When misstatements of smaller amounts could reasonably be expected to influence users' decisions, as with related party transactions or key management compensation
When the account is too large for the auditor to test completely
When the auditor wants to reduce the sample sizes for those accounts
When management requests additional assurance on specific accounts
exp: Specific materiality applies when law, regulation, the framework, or users' expectations make smaller misstatements in particular items influential, such as related party transactions, executive compensation, or industry-specific disclosures. A lower materiality increases testing, so it would never be used to reduce sample sizes.

q: Overall materiality is $100,000. Which of the following uncorrected misstatements would most likely be considered material despite being below that amount?
choices: A $40,000 understatement of a prepaid insurance balance that has no effect on any covenant
A $60,000 classification error between two operating expense lines
A $70,000 overstatement of accounts payable offset by an equal overstatement of inventory
A $40,000 overstatement of income that causes the company to meet a debt covenant it would otherwise have violated
exp: Qualitative factors under AU-C 450, such as the effect on compliance with debt covenants, can make a quantitatively small misstatement material. Misclassifications within operating expenses generally have little effect on users' decisions.

q: At the end of an audit, the auditor has identified uncorrected factual misstatements of $25,000, a $15,000 difference between management's estimate and the auditor's estimate, and projected misstatements from sampling, net of the factual misstatements found in the samples, of $40,000. All of these overstate income. What total amount should the auditor compare with materiality?
exp: AU-C 450 requires the auditor to evaluate the aggregate of factual, judgmental, and projected misstatements: $25,000 + $15,000 + $40,000 = $80,000. Leaving out either the judgmental or the projected misstatements understates the likely misstatement.

q: Management recorded an allowance for credit losses of $500,000. The auditor developed a range of reasonable outcomes from $420,000 to $470,000 and concluded that the range is supported by sufficient appropriate evidence. What is the misstatement in the allowance?
choices: $0, because the auditor's range is reasonable
exp: When management's point estimate is outside the auditor's reasonable range, the misstatement is at least the difference between management's estimate and the nearest point of the range: $500,000 - $470,000 = $30,000. Measuring to the low end of the range or to its midpoint overstates the misstatement.

q: Regarding uncorrected misstatements, the written representations the auditor obtains from management should include
choices: a statement that management will correct the misstatements in the next fiscal year
the auditor's calculation of projected misstatements for each sample
management's belief that the effects of uncorrected misstatements are immaterial, individually and in aggregate, with a summary of the items included in or attached to the letter
a statement that the auditor agrees with management's assessment of each misstatement
exp: AU-C 580 and AU-C 450 require management to represent that it believes the effects of uncorrected misstatements are immaterial, individually and in aggregate, with a summary of those items included or attached. The representation is management's, not the auditor's, and does not promise future correction.

q: Under AU-C 450, which misstatements should the auditor request management to correct?
choices: Only misstatements that individually exceed overall materiality
Only misstatements that individually exceed performance materiality
Only factual misstatements, because judgmental misstatements are a matter of opinion
All misstatements accumulated during the audit, other than those that are clearly trivial
exp: AU-C 450 requires the auditor to communicate all accumulated misstatements on a timely basis and to request that management correct them, not just those above materiality. Only clearly trivial items are excluded from accumulation. Judgmental misstatements are included as well.

q: Which of the following is an inherent risk factor as described in AU-C 315, as amended by SAS No. 145?
choices: Subjectivity in measuring an accounting estimate
Ineffective general IT controls over access to programs
The sample size the auditor plans to use for tests of details
The auditor's lack of experience in the client's industry
exp: SAS No. 145 identifies inherent risk factors as complexity, subjectivity, change, uncertainty, and susceptibility to misstatement from management bias or fraud. Ineffective IT general controls relate to control risk, and sample size relates to detection risk.

q: During risk assessment, the auditor identifies significant deficiencies in the control environment, including management's weak commitment to competent financial reporting staff. Which overall response to this financial statement-level risk is most appropriate?
choices: Assess control risk below the maximum to offset the weak control environment
Perform more substantive procedures at interim dates to spread the work evenly
Reduce the involvement of experienced staff so that procedures are performed independently of management
Perform more audit procedures as of the period end rather than at an interim date
exp: AU-C 330 says that a weak control environment may call for overall responses, such as performing more procedures at period-end, obtaining more extensive evidence, assigning more experienced staff, increasing supervision, and adding unpredictability. Relying more on interim work assumes controls carry the results forward to period-end, which a weak environment does not support.

q: In which situation would an auditor most likely set performance materiality at a lower percentage of overall materiality?
choices: The client has stable operations and no misstatements were identified in prior audits
The entity's accounts are few and individually large
The client has a history of numerous misstatements identified in prior audits
The auditor plans to rely on controls that were effective in prior years
exp: Performance materiality reduces the probability that uncorrected and undetected misstatements together exceed materiality. Expecting more misstatements, based on history, calls for a lower performance materiality. A clean history and effective controls support a higher percentage.

q: A company's pretax income has fluctuated between small losses and small profits over the past five years, while revenues have been stable at about $50,000,000. Which benchmark is most likely appropriate for overall materiality?
choices: Total revenues or a normalized earnings measure rather than current-year pretax income
Current-year pretax income, because it is always the preferred benchmark for for-profit entities
Total liabilities, because creditors are the primary users
The smallest account balance in the trial balance
exp: AU-C 320 guidance notes that when profit is volatile or near breakeven, a stable benchmark such as revenues or normalized earnings may be more appropriate. Using a near-zero pretax income would produce an unrealistically low materiality.

q: In an audit performed under PCAOB standards, AS 2105 requires that tolerable misstatement for an individual account or disclosure be
choices: equal to materiality for the financial statements as a whole
less than materiality for the financial statements as a whole
determined by applying a fixed percentage of the account's balance
approved by the audit committee before fieldwork begins
exp: AS 2105 requires tolerable misstatement at the account or disclosure level to be less than materiality for the financial statements as a whole, so that the misstatements across accounts are not material in total. No fixed percentage is prescribed, and the audit committee does not approve it.

q: Which of the following is most likely to reduce nonsampling risk in an audit?
choices: Increasing sample sizes for tests of details
Using statistical rather than nonstatistical sampling methods
Proper planning, supervision, and review of the engagement team's work
Increasing tolerable misstatement for the accounts tested
exp: Nonsampling risk comes from inappropriate procedures or misinterpreted evidence and is reduced by planning, supervision, review, and quality management. Larger samples and statistical methods address sampling risk instead.

q: Holding audit risk constant, an auditor reduces overall materiality because the financial statements will be used in connection with a proposed sale of the company. The most likely effect is that
choices: more audit evidence is needed, such as larger sample sizes for tests of details
less audit evidence is needed, because users will be more knowledgeable
the assessed inherent risk will decrease
detection risk will increase
exp: Materiality and the amount of evidence are inversely related. A lower materiality requires more evidence so the auditor can detect smaller misstatements. It does not change inherent risk, and detection risk must decrease, not increase.

q: In a group audit, the group auditor determines materiality to be used for the work on a significant component. That materiality should be
choices: equal to materiality for the group financial statements for every component, so results are comparable
higher than group materiality, because each component is smaller than the group
set by component management and accepted by the group auditor
lower than materiality for the group financial statements as a whole, to reduce aggregation risk
exp: Under AU-C 600, materiality for work at components is set below group materiality so that the probability of the aggregate of misstatements across components exceeding group materiality is acceptably low. Using group materiality at each component ignores aggregation risk.

q: A company's senior executives receive large bonuses only if earnings per share meet aggressive targets that analysts consider unlikely. In the fraud triangle described in AU-C 240, this circumstance is primarily an example of
choices: an opportunity to commit fraud
an incentive or pressure to commit fraud
an attitude or rationalization
a weakness in the monitoring component of internal control
exp: Compensation tied to aggressive targets creates an incentive or pressure for fraudulent financial reporting. Opportunity relates to weak controls or complex transactions, and attitude relates to management's willingness to justify dishonest acts.

q: Ending inventory in the prior year was overstated by $30,000, and the misstatement was not corrected. In the current year, the auditor identifies an uncorrected $50,000 overstatement of current-year revenue. Considering both items, what is the net effect on current-year pretax income?
choices: $20,000 overstatement
$80,000 overstatement
$50,000 overstatement
$20,000 understatement
exp: The prior-year overstatement of ending inventory overstates current-year beginning inventory and cost of sales, understating current income by $30,000. Combined with the $50,000 revenue overstatement, the net effect is a $20,000 overstatement. Adding the two amounts ignores that the inventory error reverses in the current year.

q: Under AU-C 315, as amended by SAS No. 145, an assertion is a relevant assertion when
choices: the related account balance exceeds overall materiality
management has designed controls over the assertion
it has an identified risk of material misstatement, meaning there is a reasonable possibility of a misstatement occurring that could be material
the auditor intends to rely on controls related to the assertion
exp: SAS No. 145 defines a relevant assertion as one with an identified RMM, which exists when a misstatement is reasonably possible and could be material. Account size alone does not make an assertion relevant, and relevance does not depend on whether controls exist or will be relied on.

q: An auditor assesses the risk of material misstatement as low for all assertions related to a material prepaid expenses balance. Under AU-C 330, the auditor
choices: may omit substantive procedures for the balance, because the RMM is low
should still design and perform substantive procedures for the material account balance
should test controls over prepaid expenses instead of performing substantive procedures
may rely solely on inquiry of management about the balance
exp: AU-C 330 requires substantive procedures for each material class of transactions, account balance, and disclosure regardless of the assessed RMM. This reflects the judgmental nature of risk assessment and the inherent limitations of internal control. Inquiry alone is never sufficient.

q: A retailer initiates, records, and processes most of its sales electronically with no manual intervention or documentation outside the IT system. For the occurrence and completeness of sales, the auditor most likely will need to
choices: perform only substantive analytical procedures on sales
vouch a large sample of sales to paper shipping documents
rely on management's representations about the system's reliability
test the operating effectiveness of relevant controls, because substantive procedures alone cannot provide sufficient appropriate evidence
exp: AU-C 315 and AU-C 330 recognize that when transactions are processed in highly automated systems with little documentation outside the system, substantive procedures alone may not be sufficient, so the auditor must test controls. Paper documents may not exist, and representations do not substitute for evidence.

q: Under AU-C 320, which of the following must the auditor include in the audit documentation regarding materiality?
choices: Materiality for the financial statements as a whole, any lower specific materiality levels, performance materiality, the factors considered in determining them, and any revisions
Only the final materiality amount used at the end of the audit
Management's approval of the materiality amounts
The materiality amounts used by other firms auditing companies in the same industry
exp: AU-C 320 requires documentation of overall materiality, any specific materiality levels, performance materiality, the factors considered, and any revisions as the audit progressed. Management does not approve the auditor's materiality judgments.

q: For one assertion, the auditor assesses inherent risk as high and, after testing operating effectiveness, control risk as low. For a second assertion, both inherent risk and control risk are high. Compared with the second assertion, the acceptable detection risk for the first assertion is
choices: lower, so the auditor must perform more extensive substantive tests
the same, because inherent risk is high for both
higher, so less persuasive substantive evidence may be sufficient
zero, because effective controls replace substantive procedures
exp: Effective controls lower the RMM for the first assertion, which permits higher acceptable detection risk and less persuasive or less extensive substantive procedures than when both risks are high. Detection risk can never be zero, because substantive procedures are always required for material items.
